'''''Glebionis coronaria''''', formerly called ''Chrysanthemum coronarium'', is a species of flowering plant in the family [[Asteraceae]]. It is native to the [[Mediterranean Basin|Mediterranean]] region.<ref>[http://luirig.altervista.org/flora/taxa/index1.php?scientific-name=glebionis+coronaria Altervista Flora Italiana, ''Glebionis coronaria'' (L.) Spach] includes photos and European distribution map</ref> It is cultivated and naturalized in [[East Asia]] and in scattered locations in North America.<ref>{{cite web |url= http://www.efloras.org/florataxon.aspx?flora_id=2&taxon_id=250058139 |title= ''Glebionis coronaria'' (Linnaeus) Cassini ex Spach, 1841. <big>茼蒿</big> tong hao |date= n.d. |website= Flora of China |publisher= eFloras |volume=20-21 |page=653, 772}}</ref><ref>[http://bonap.net/MapGallery/County/Glebionis%20coronaria.png Biota of North America Program 2014 county distribution map]</ref>

''Glebionis coronaria'' is used as a [[leaf vegetable]]. [[English language]] common names include '''garland chrysanthemum''',<ref name=GRIN>{{GRIN | ''Glebionis coronaria'' | 417417 | access-date = 30 July 2014}}</ref> '''chrysanthemum greens''',<ref name=GRIN/> '''edible chrysanthemum''', '''crowndaisy chrysanthemum''',<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://nature.go.kr/kbi/plant/pilbk/selectPlantPilbkDtl.do?plantPilbkNo=30125|title=쑥갓|website=Korea Biodiversity Information System|publisher=[[Korea National Arboretum]]|language=ko|trans-title=crowndaisy chrysanthemum|access-date=7 December 2016}}</ref> '''chop suey greens''',<ref name=GRIN/> '''crown daisy''',<ref name=GRIN/> and '''Japanese greens'''.<ref name=GRIN/>

''Glebionis coronaria'' has been hybridized with related ''[[Argyranthemum]]'' species to create [[cultivar]]s of [[garden marguerite]]s.<ref name=FlorShawWats18>{{Citation |last1=Flores |first1=Anita |last2=Shaw |first2=Julian |last3=Watson |first3=John |date=2018 |title=Unpicking a daisy chain |journal=The Plantsman |series=New Series |volume=17 |issue=4 |pages=238–243  |name-list-style=amp }}</ref>

== Characteristics ==
A [[leaf]]y [[herb#Botanical definitions|herb]], the garland chrysanthemum is an [[annual plant]]. It has yellow ray florets grouped in small [[pseudanthium|flower heads]] and aromatic, bipinnately [[Leaf shape|lobed]] leaves. Its seeds are ribbed and winged [[cypselae]].<ref>{{cite web |url= http://www.efloras.org/florataxon.aspx?flora_id=1&taxon_id=250058139 |title= ''Glebionis coronaria'' (Linnaeus) Cassini ex Spach, 1841. Crown daisy, garland chrysanthemum |date= n.d. |website= Flora of North America  |publisher= eFloras |volume= 19-21 |page= 555 |access-date=<!-- might be too far down page history -->}}</ref> The vegetable grows very well in mild or slightly cold climates, but will go quickly into premature flowering in warm summer conditions. Seeds are sown in early spring and fall.{{Citation needed|date=July 2021}}

"The plant is rich in minerals and vitamins with potassium concentrations at 610 mg/100 g and carotene at 3.4 g/100 g in edible portions. In addition, the plant contains various antioxidants (in stem, leaf, and root tissues) that have potential long-term benefits for human health, although toxic (dioxin) properties have also been observed. Extracts from ''C. coronarium'' var. ''spatiosum'' have been shown to inhibit growth of ''[[Lactobacillus casei]]'', a beneficial human intestinal bacterium."<ref>{{cite journal |last1= Teixeira da Silva |first1= Jaime A. |last2= Yonekura |first2= Lina |last3= Kaganda |first3= Joyceline |last4= Mookdasanit |first4= Juta |last5= Nhut |first5= Duong T. |last6= Afach |first6= Ghanwa |year= 2005 |title= Important secondary metabolites and essential oils of species within the Anthemideae (Asteraceae) |journal= Journal of Herbs, Spices & Medicinal Plants |volume= 11 |issue= 1 |pages= 1–4 |doi= 10.1300/J044v11n01_01|s2cid= 84752321 }}</ref>

{{Clear|left}}

The plant's greens are used in many Asian cuisines. Normally only the greens are consumed but the stronger tasting stalk can also be used. They can be simmered, steamed, stir fried, deep fried, or added to soups. When overcooked they can become bitter.<ref name= "Cook's Guide" />

In [[Korean cuisine]], the plant is called ''ssukgat'' (쑥갓) and is used as an ingredient in various soups and stews, as well as a side dish (''[[namul]]''). 

In [[Chinese cuisine]], it is called ''tóng hāo cài'' (茼蒿菜) in Mandarin, and ''tong ho choy'' in Cantonese. It is used as an ingredient for stir-fries, stews, casseroles, and hotpots.<ref>{{cite web |url= https://www.diversivore.com/ingredient-pages/garland-chrysanthemum |title= How to Find, Choose, & Use Garland Chrysanthemum |date= n.d. |website= Diversivore |access-date= 22 September 2020 }}</ref> In traditional food culture it is seen as "warming" and thus was primarily eaten when it was cold.<ref name= "Cook's Guide" />

In [[Japanese cuisine]], it is called ''shungiku'' (春菊 "spring chrysanthemum"), and is used in ''[[nabemono]],'' mixed into rice, or drizzled with soy sauce and sesame seeds as a side dish.{{Cn|date=October 2024}} It is also commonly added to [[sukiyaki]].<ref name= "Cook's Guide" >{{cite book |last1=Hutton |first1=Wendy |title=A Cook's Guide to Asian Vegetables |date=2004 |publisher=Periplus Editions |location=Singapore |isbn=0794600786 |pages=46–47}}</ref>

In [[Vietnamese cuisine]], the greens are known as ''cải cúc'' or ''tần ô'', and are used in soup (''canh'') or as a side dish accompanying various noodle soups. In a hotpot, it is added at the last moment to the pot to avoid overcooking.{{Citation needed|date=July 2021}}

In [[Crete]], a variety of the species called ''mantilida'' (μαντηλίδα) has its tender shoots eaten raw or steamed by the locals (see [[Greek cuisine]]).{{Citation needed|date=July 2021}}
